source.title_on_document: Empowering Engineering Students Through Artificial Intelligence (AI): Blended Human–AI Creative Ideation Processes With ChatGPT

supplement.where: No supplementary material or appendix is referenced in the document; the PDF ends with references on p. 19.
supplement.holds: No supplement identified. The direct assistance comparison is shown graphically in Figure 7 (p. 11); numerical test results in Table 4 (p. 11) instead concern prior ChatGPT experience.

paper_design_summary: Third-year industrial design and product development engineering students were randomly assigned to opposite orders of ChatGPT-assisted and unaided ideation, switching conditions between a public-transport task and a university-spaces task (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1). The analyzed cohort comprised 51 students and produced 728 sketched and briefly described ideas; students subsequently assessed peers' ideas for creativity, innovation, viability, user benefits, value, complexity, and overall quality (p. 4, section 4.1; pp. 5 and 8, Table 1 and section 4.3.2; pp. 14 and 16, sections 6-7). A non-randomized comparison of previous ChatGPT experience uses the same study's AI-assisted outputs (pp. 9 and 11, section 5 and Table 4).

studies.label: Controlled crossover experiment: public transport and university-space ideation

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly assigned to groups determining assistance order. Group A completed T1 without ChatGPT and T2 with ChatGPT; Group B completed T1 with ChatGPT and T2 without ChatGPT. Task order was fixed, while AI-condition order was randomized. Prior ChatGPT experience, examined separately in Table 4, was not assigned.
assignment.quote: For the experiment, students were randomly assigned to two groups and placed in classrooms based on their respective group assignments:
assignment.locator: pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1; p. 11, Table 4 for the experience subgroups
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration or registration reference is stated in the full document (pp. 1–19).

arms.name: ChatGPT-assisted ideation
arms.description: Experimental condition: supervised use of ChatGPT on university-provided computers; other websites and tools restricted. Group B receives this condition in T1 and Group A in T2. These are condition labels, not independent groups of people across both tasks (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1).

arms.name: Unaided ideation
arms.description: Control condition: supervised ideation in a computer-free classroom without external support. Group A receives this condition in T1; Group B receives it in T2 after its earlier ChatGPT use (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1).

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition are reported. The paper reports 51 participants and explicitly describes its results as deriving from this cohort, but gives no separate number at random assignment or per-sequence participant counts. Table 4 reports n = 80 and n = 280 ideas for its prior-experience comparison, not participant counts; its relation to the experimental-condition subtotal of 368 ideas in Table 3 is unexplained (pp. 4, 7, 11 and 16).
participants.who: Third-year undergraduates in the Bachelor's Degree in Engineering specializing in Industrial Design and Product Development at Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya · BarcelonaTech (UPC); the participating students also evaluated peers' outputs (p. 4, section 4.1; p. 8, section 4.3.2; p. 16, section 7).
participants.country: Spain (study institution; p. 1 affiliations and p. 4, Section 4.1). Participant nationality is not stated.
participants.quote: The results of this research primarily derive from a cohort of 51 engineering students specializing in Industrial Design and Product Development.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 4.1; p. 16, section 7 (cohort underlying the results and 51 evaluators)

ai_tool.how_used: Students were instructed to use the text chatbot to support ideation. It answered questions, offered explanations and background information, and suggested directions for creative work; no standardized or reproduced prompts are described. Access to other websites and tools was restricted (p. 7, section 4.3.1).

task.description: T1: generate innovative ideas to improve public transport. T2: generate innovative ideas to improve university spaces. Students were asked for eight unique ideas per task, each expressed as a sketch and brief description on an A5 template (p. 6, section 4.3.1).
task.duration: 30 min per task, with conditions and classrooms reversed after T1 (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1).

outcomes.name: Creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Anonymous peer ratings by participating third-year students, excluding self-evaluation; raters were students rather than an independent expert panel. Items used a 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 4 (Strongly Agree) scale. Three items: Is creative; Solves the problem in an original way; Is unconventional. Cronbach's alpha = 0.83. Instrument and scale: p. 5, section 4.2.1 and Table 1; rating procedure: p. 8, section 4.3.2. Figure 7 reports this measure for T1, T2 and the total; exact plotted values and the meaning of error bars are not specified. The AI-assisted condition had ChatGPT available during production. Its T2 unaided comparator was produced after prior AI use, while its T1 comparator preceded any experimental AI exposure (pp. 6-7, Figure 1). The additional prior-experience contrast below is observational, uses AI-assisted ideas from the same experiment, and is not the randomized assistance effect (p. 11, Table 4). The 728 units denote the full peer-assessed idea corpus, not a verified count for each subgroup test (p. 14, Section 6, Research question 2).
outcomes.delay: Ideas were produced in the first experimental session and rated in a second session; the interval between sessions is not stated (pp. 6–8, Section 4.3). The later rating session is not a delayed creative-production task.

contrasts.reported: The paper reports no significant differences in peer evaluations between ideas generated with and without ChatGPT (Mann-Whitney test). Figure 7 shows T1, T2 and total bars, but no exact numerical condition means, SDs, test statistics, p-values, or error-bar values are printed for this contrast. The text describes slightly higher scores with ChatGPT in T1 and higher scores without ChatGPT in T2 (p. 9, section 5). No SEs are supplied, and the Figure 7 error bars are undefined; the pooled comparison combines pre-exposure and post-exposure unaided controls (p. 7, Figure 1).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Possible shared sample with c031, Evaluating AI-assisted creative ideation: A crossover study in higher education (DOI 10.1016/j.tsc.2025.101958). Both reports describe 51 third-year UPC industrial design and product development engineering students, the same two tasks and opposite assistance orders, and the same idea counts: unaided T1 = 158 and T2 = 202; assisted T1 = 195 and T2 = 173; total = 728. These source matches strongly suggest overlap, but do not establish participant identity. Author confirmation is needed before treating the papers as independent samples; c031 participant counts and statistics are not substituted for c201 values.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. Students were explicitly randomly assigned to groups that followed opposite orders of ChatGPT-assisted and unaided ideation (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1). The analyzed cohort comprises 51 people, only just above the 50-person threshold; the paper explicitly links its results to this cohort (p. 4, section 4.1; p. 16, section 7). The 728 ideas are outputs, not additional participants (p. 7, Table 3). Creativity and related dimensions were peer-rated on those outputs (p. 5, Table 1; p. 8, section 4.3.2; p. 14, section 6, Research question 2). Missing numerical assistance-effect estimates, unreported participant-adjusted precision and potential overlap with c031 affect extraction, pooling or sample deduplication, not these eligibility criteria. The prior-experience contrast in Table 4 is observational, and the T2 unaided comparator follows prior AI use.

one_line_finding: Among 51 analyzed students who produced 728 ideas, ChatGPT assistance showed no significant peer-rated differences, while an observational prior-experience comparison found higher overall scores for experienced users (3.00 [SD 0.82] versus 2.75 [SD 0.94], p = 0.039; p. 16, Section 7; p. 7, Table 3; p. 9, Section 5; p. 11, Figure 7 and Table 4).
open_questions: The allocation method beyond random assignment, the number randomized, and the participant count in each sequence are not supplied (pp. 4 and 6-7, sections 4.1 and 4.3.1).

Figure 7 supplies no exact numerical means, SDs, test statistics, p-values, or defined error-bar values for the assistance contrast. Numeric values would require the data; the plotted bars were not digitized (pp. 9 and 11, section 5 and Figure 7).

The AI-assisted prior-experience analysis lists n = 80 and n = 280 ideas in Table 4, whereas Table 3 gives 368 experimental-condition ideas. The document does not reconcile these counts or report subgroup participant counts (pp. 7 and 11).
Mann-Whitney tests are described for idea evaluations, without reported participant clustering, paired/crossover adjustment, or a participant-level standard error (p. 9, section 4.4; p. 11, Table 4).

The T2 unaided outputs were produced after Group B lost ChatGPT access. No washout or separate carryover analysis is described, and no comparison with both groups working unassisted after different AI exposure is reported (pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1; p. 11, Figure 7).

Possible shared participants with c031: the cohort size, institution, degree, tasks, assistance orders and four task-by-condition idea counts match, but participant identity is unconfirmed (c201 pp. 4 and 6-7, sections 4.1 and 4.3.1, Figure 1 and Table 3; c031 pp. 4-5, sections 3.1 and 3.2.1 and Figure 1). Author confirmation is needed for sample deduplication.
notes:
The markdown was read from beginning to end, including all references; it contains no appendix. Relevant PDF text and the rendered figures/tables on pp. 7 and 11 were checked. This is one experiment with two tasks and a later rating session, not two independent samples. Coded lab_rct because the documented setting is a controlled, supervised session in separate classrooms; the article does not establish that this was ordinary coursework (pp. 6-8). Arms name the current assistance conditions; sequence membership reverses across tasks. The with_ai records describe the current-assistance comparisons in Figure 7, with its T1, T2 and total panels retained as variants of each measure. Specifically, the T2 unaided comparator is after_ai work, not an AI-naive control; the paper supplies no separate after_ai effect. Rating in the second session does not make the original production outcome delayed. The seven rated outcomes are recorded separately; the eighth outcome preserves the descriptive idea counts in Table 3, which are not a tested participant-level fluency effect. Complexity is coded other because it concerns interacting concepts and details, not simply output length. Overall assessment is coded usefulness because its item is Is a good idea, rather than an explicit overall-creativity rating (p. 5, Table 1). The observational prior-experience comparisons are retained as comparison_type other within the same outcome records; their means, SDs and r values must not be used as AI-versus-no-AI statistics. No standardized effect was computed. The n_units = 728 in each rated outcome refers to the complete peer-assessed idea corpus (p. 14, section 6); Table 4 subgroup idea counts are given separately. Self-reported perceptions and qualitative concerns about homogeneity are not scored diversity outcomes and were not entered as such (p. 6, Table 2; pp. 9-14, results and Table 5). The c201 document does not explicitly state sample reuse; finalization identified possible overlap with c031, as detailed in sample_overlap. Data and materials are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request; no data or code URL is supplied (p. 17, Data Availability Statement).

Reconciliation: Both raw forms parsed. The full markdown, including all references, was read; PDF pp. 1, 4–9, 11, 14, 16–17 were checked directly with PyMuPDF. Figures 1 and 7 were inspected from their PDF images. No supplement or appendix is referenced. The number at randomization and per-sequence participant counts remain null. Core inclusion uses the 51-person cohort explicitly linked to the results, not the number of ideas or ratings.

The Results section additionally states that prior-experience groups did not differ significantly when working without ChatGPT, but gives no exact statistics for that unaided comparison (p. 9, Section 5). This result is retained as a narrative comparison of the same rated outcomes; no additional outcome family or separate after_ai estimate is inferred. The with_ai outcome records describe current-assistance comparisons and the assisted outputs. Group B's T2 unaided output series is after-AI work, and the pooled Figure 7 comparison mixes pre-exposure and post-exposure unaided controls. No separate after_ai effect comparing unassisted post-exposure work with unassisted unexposed work is reported or derived.

Substantive information omissions are counted as differences: six reliability statistics present only in A, descriptive task directions for three outcomes present only in A, the unaided prior-experience result noted only in B, and the additional prior-experience finding in B's one-line summary. A null in a reliability difference means B omitted that statistic; it does not mean B disputed it. Equivalent arm labels, paraphrases, locator formatting, empty versus explanatory not-stated fields, and details recorded elsewhere in both forms are not counted. Both screeners otherwise agree on design, assignment, arms, participant counts, tool, task, all outcome coding fields, all Table 3 and Table 4 numbers, supplement status, overlap status, company involvement and each eligibility decision. n_unresolved counts unresolved differences between screeners; shared source-data gaps remain in open_questions. No effect size was computed, no graph values were estimated, and no external source was used.

Finalization (2026-10-09): Read the complete c201 markdown through the references (706 lines); the 19-page PDF contains no appendix or embedded attachment and references no supplement. Rechecked eligibility passages and every recorded Table 1, Table 3 and Table 4 value against PDF text; inspected Figures 1 and 7 directly. All three challenge files have empty problems arrays, so challenge_resolution is empty and the challenge counts are zero. All reconciliation differences were already resolved; the reconciliation object is unchanged. The people checker also flagged possible overlap with c031 in its confirmed observations. Independent checks of the c031 title, methods and Figure 1 support this as an unresolved sample-identity question, now recorded in sample_overlap, open_questions and final.open_items. All open items concern reporting, effect extraction, interpretation or sample deduplication; none leaves an eligibility criterion unsettled. The source already supplies the current supplement field and the appropriate lab_rct design class. Unreported randomization and arm counts remain null, no effect size was computed, and no plotted value was estimated. open_items.item: Allocation method, number randomized and per-sequence participant counts are unreported (open_questions[0]; pp. 4 and 6-7). Authors could provide the allocation protocol and participant flow. This does not unsettle criterion 1, because random assignment is explicit, or criterion 2, because p. 16 links the analyzed results to 51 students.

Exact assistance-versus-unaided means, SDs, tests, p-values and the definition of Figure 7 error bars are unavailable (open_questions[1]; pp. 9 and 11). Authors could supply the numerical results and underlying data; p. 17 offers data and materials upon reasonable request. This affects effect extraction, not eligibility.

Table 4 lists 80 and 280 ideas for the prior-experience subgroups, whereas Table 3 reports 368 assisted ideas; subgroup participant counts and the reason for the discrepancy are unreported (open_questions[2]; pp. 7 and 11). Authors could reconcile the analysis rows and provide subgroup participant counts. This concerns an observational subgroup analysis and does not contradict the 51-person analyzed cohort used for criterion 2.

Participant clustering, paired/crossover adjustment and participant-level uncertainty are not reported for the idea-evaluation comparisons (open_questions[3]; p. 9, section 4.4; p. 11, Table 4). Authors could clarify the analysis and provide linked participant, task and rating data or appropriately adjusted estimates. This affects pooling and precision, not eligibility.

Washout and carryover handling are unreported, and the T2 unaided condition follows prior ChatGPT use (open_questions[4]; pp. 6-7, section 4.3.1 and Figure 1). Authors could clarify timing and carryover procedures and supply results by task and randomized sequence. The reported design has no separate comparison of unassisted exposed and unexposed groups, so no isolated after_ai effect is recorded; randomized assistance order still meets criterion 1.

Possible shared sample with c031 remains unconfirmed despite matching cohort, procedure and task-by-condition idea counts (open_questions[5]; c201 pp. 4 and 6-7; c031 pp. 4-5, including Figure 1). Authors could confirm whether the same students and outputs were reused and specify the overlap. This affects sample deduplication, not the three within-study eligibility criteria.
